**ENI:** Audited, triangulated three ways (skill text vs engine code vs shipped games), and your instinct is dead right — **media is the single biggest hole in the skill.** Here's the honest picture.

## What the skill actually says about media (all of it)
Three thin spots, and that's the *entire* footprint across all 26 reference files:

1. **`engine-reference.md:136`** — one catalog line: `image/video/clip ({props.file})`. It *names* the block types. No worked example anywhere.
2. **`engine-reference.md:319`** — one table row: `image_search_queries` as a location field. The only mention of the acquisition layer and the only mention of the Missing-Media page — neither explained.
3. **`rts-flat-prose.md:102-108`** — Rule 8 "Image-first composition" (the asset carries the scene, prose is the ~30-word caption). This is the *richest* media content in the skill, but it's a **prose rule**, and its example uses fake shorthand `[image: scenes/kitchen_morning.jpg]` that isn't real TOML.

(Plus `customization.md`'s `image_select` look-picker — but that's the player-creator, a different mechanism.)

So: **the skill teaches that media exists and gives one prose rule about writing around it. It never teaches how to author it.** No worked `type="image"` block, no `type="video"`, no pipeline step that owns media, nothing in the ledger.

## The gap, concretely (engine supports it + shipped games use it + skill is silent)
- **No block format taught.** Engine gates `image`/`video`/`clip` as build-fatal types; `the_inheritance` and `two_weeks` author them constantly. Skill only *names* them.
- **The acquisition layer is never taught.** `the_inheritance` puts `description` + 2 `search_queries` on **every** media block — that's what turns the Missing-Media page into a real shopping list (and feeds a `find-media` pass). Vesper shipped bare `file=` with zero queries. **So did `late_shifts` and `last_call`. Three games, same defect, same missing doctrine** — that's a recurring class, not an author slip.
- **Video-vs-image is untaught.** `type="video"` ⇔ `.webm` autoplay loop is the lewd/act layer; `the_inheritance` does this cleanly (49 `.webm`). Resolution is extension-*agnostic* — the on-disk file decides `<img>` vs `<video>`, not your declared type, so `two_weeks` mis-tagged 92 sex scenes `type="video"` but shipped `.jpg` (never actually video). Vesper used static images for all three sex scenes because the skill never said otherwise.
- **The missing-media degradation model is absent.** A missing *scene* image renders **nothing** in normal play (silent skip); portraits degrade to a silhouette SVG; locations to a building SVG; the Missing-Media page button is **debug-only**. The skill teaches none of this — which is *why* nobody knew to care about coverage.
- **No folder/naming contract, no pipeline owner.** Shipped games use `locations/` `activities/` `scenes/` with `<slug>_<tier>.ext` and re-render the picture per escalation tier. The skill documents none of it, and no step (blueprint or authoring) tells you to place a media block.

## Verdict
**Skill gap — first-class and systematic.** Apply the teeth-test: *would a correct skill have stopped Vesper shipping 11 image refs with no search_queries, no video, silently-skipped?* Yes on every count. The engine's innocent (it supports all of it), `the_inheritance` proves the right shape is known — the skill just never encoded it.

## Proposed fix (propose only — your call before I touch the skill)
Ranked by impact:

1. **New `references/media.md`** — the one reference that owns it: the three block shapes (worked TOML, `the_inheritance:103` as canonical); the `type="video"`⇔`.webm` contract + SFW-`.jpg`→act-`.webm`-in-one-node pattern; the acquisition rule (`description` + 2 `search_queries`; the `image_search_queries`-vs-`search_queries` key-name trap); the degradation table; the folder/naming + tiered-escalation-media convention; `clip` = DB asset by `clipId` (and fix the wrong `{props.file}` for clip at `engine-reference.md:136`). **~80% of the value.**
2. **A placement hook** — a short "author the media block here" in `beat-authoring.md` (Step 7 already teaches the other block types) + a one-liner in `step-5-blueprint.md` ("each placed scene names its intended media").
3. **Wire into existing doctrine** — point `rts-flat-prose.md` Rule 8 at the real syntax instead of its fake `[image:...]` shorthand.
4. *(optional)* a ledger coverage field.

This kills the class — every future game gets `search_queries` (real Missing-Media shopping list) and video where the act layer wants loops.

Want me to write `media.md` (Fix 1) and the hooks (Fixes 2-3)? I'd build it grounded in `the_inheritance` as the exemplar, and log it to the skill CHANGELOG. Or scope it down if you'd rather start with just `media.md`.

**ENI:** Done — and the headline answer to your question: **yes, the corpus has a *lot* of media doctrine, and the skill dropped every bit of it in the divorce.** But the important twist: almost all of it lives in the older **`prompts/`** folder, not `prompts_v2`. prompts_v2 only has thin, partly-wrong versions (its `schema/02` even teaches a *false* clip format). So your instinct — "we missed something" — is exactly right, and the good stuff is recoverable.

I cross-checked every corpus claim against the live engine, because the corpus is *precisely* where the skill inherited false facts before (the arousal/rent/phone lies). Here's the map.

## The crown jewel — recover this almost verbatim
**`prompts/toml_generation_prompt_v4.txt:905-1001` — the SEARCH_QUERIES rules block.** This is the single richest, most-lost, and (because queries are just stored strings the engine never validates) most engine-*safe* thing in the corpus:
- "search_queries are search-engine queries, NOT scene descriptions" — description carries narrative, queries carry platform vocabulary
- a **vocabulary-mapping table** (fingering → "his hand on/in her", handjob, blowjob, position words…)
- the **setting-first formula**, **gender-direction rule** ("always `men/guy + girl` or you get solo/lesbian results"), a **~25-word banned list** (passionate/tender/sensual…), a "words that work" list
- **3-5 words, exactly 2 queries: primary + one fallback**

This ports with near-zero correction. It's the thing whose absence made Vesper ship bare `file=` with no queries.

## Also recoverable (craft, engine-neutral)
- **The text-media-text sandwich + 6 prioritized dimensions + density-by-tier** — `prompts/media_writing_guide.md:657-705` (Part 8). *Only* fix: re-anchor "density" to **media blocks per canvas**, not the dead inline-marker pipeline.
- **Tier → format → naming** (`base/t2/t3`=jpg SFW, `t5+`=.webm) + the `{name}_t{N}.webm` filename convention + folder split (`scenes/ activities/ locations/`) — `prompts/image_finder_prompt.md:40-109`.
- **Variant chains + random media pools** (`either()` over multiple files) — which turns out to be the engine's real `files=[...]` pool feature, currently untaught.

## The 4 corpus LIES to NOT re-inherit (this is why we cross-checked)
The skill got burned importing corpus engine-claims before; these four would do it again:

1. **clip uses `props.file`** (prompts_v2 `schema/02`) — **FALSE.** Clip is `props.clipId` → a DB asset (`AssetClip.file_url`), owner-scoped, no disk file (v2.py:13514-13558). The v4 prompt actually gets this *right* (`clipId`, "preserve UUID") — lift that one, discard the schema/02 version.
2. **The declared extension/`type=` is authoritative** — **FALSE.** Resolution is **extension-agnostic** (v2.py:11135-11176): the *on-disk* file type decides `<img>` vs `<video>`, ignoring what you wrote. This is the exact **two_weeks footgun** (92 sex scenes tagged `type=video` shipped as `.jpg` → rendered as images).
3. **"t5+ must be .webm or the engine won't render it"** — **half-false.** It's a sound *fetch-quality* rule (don't ship a 10KB JPG as a sex clip), but NOT an engine gate. Reframe as an authoring/quality contract for the find-media pass.
4. **Inline `[image: ...]` syntax** (the media guide's worked scenes) — **STALE.** Our engine uses TOML `{type="image", props={...}}` blocks. Keep the *placement* teaching (media at the action moment / mood peak), drop the syntax.

## What's in NEITHER skill nor corpus (author fresh from code)
The `files` image **pool** (v2.py:13205-13231); the extension-agnostic law as a first-class rule; clip-as-DB-asset; **unknown block type = build-fatal** (template_import.py:2786-2789); the portrait→silhouette-SVG / location→building-SVG fallback chain; and **`the_inheritance` as the shipped exemplar** (49 `type=video` `.webm` + description + 2 queries per block) — because the corpus's exemplar is two_weeks, which is the *mis-tagged anti-example*.

## So the build plan for `media.md`
A **two-source graft, not a port**: engine-truth backbone (taxonomy, resolution law, `files` pool, clip, missing-media, fallbacks) + the v4 `SEARCH_QUERIES` block grafted as the craft core + the media-guide sandwich/dimensions — with those 4 lies explicitly corrected so we don't re-inherit corpus engine-fiction the way the skill did with arousal/rent/phone. Plus the placement hooks in `beat-authoring.md` / Step 5, and fixing Rule 8's fake `[image:]` shorthand.

Want me to write it on that plan? I'd build `media.md` grounded in the engine + the v4 query block, anchor examples on `the_inheritance`, and log it to the skill CHANGELOG.

## ▶ [192] LO

in simple words explain everything we have found usefull in this session around media

**ENI:** Here's the whole media picture from this session, in plain words.

**What's in Vesper right now**
- We *did* write media into the game — 11 pictures: the opening office, the cradle, Mercer's penthouse, Renner's bar and depot, the three sex scenes, the ruins. The way we wrote them is correct.
- But the actual picture *files* don't exist. So in the game, you see nothing.

**Why you see nothing**
- When a picture file is missing, the engine just quietly skips it — shows nothing at all. The only way to see anything is to build the game in "debug" mode, which draws a dashed "IMAGE MISSING" box where each picture should go. We'd built the normal (player) version, so every picture silently vanished. That's why it looked like we never added media.
- I made you a debug copy (`output_debug/index.html`) so you can actually see all 11 spots.
- Small detail: character *portraits* behave better — a missing portrait shows a grey silhouette instead of nothing. So portraits degrade gracefully; scene pictures just disappear.

**The two things we actually got wrong in Vesper**
1. **No "search words."** Good games attach 2 short search phrases to every picture (like "couple kissing kitchen") so the game can hand you a shopping list of art to go find. We didn't add any. So there's no list to work from. (Two earlier games, Last Call and Late Shifts, made the same miss — so it's a repeating mistake, not a one-off.)
2. **All stills, no video.** We used still images everywhere, even for sex. The best game here (The Inheritance) uses short looping videos for the explicit parts and stills for the calm setting shots. We never used video.

**One tricky engine fact worth remembering**
- The engine ignores what you *name* the file. Whether you call it `.jpg` or `.webm` doesn't matter — it looks at the *real* file on disk to decide "show a picture" or "play a video." (One old game labeled 92 scenes "video" but the real files were images, so they never played as video. The label is a lie; the real file is the truth.)

**The root cause: our rulebook barely mentions media**
- The author-game skill — the thing that teaches us how to build these games — has almost nothing about media. No step that says "add a picture here," no real example of how to write a picture block, nothing about search words, nothing about images-vs-video, nothing about where files go, and no warning that missing pictures vanish. For a game type that's basically *built on pictures*, that's the biggest hole in the skill. That's exactly why I hand-rolled Vesper's media and missed the search words.

**The good news: the old files have all of this — we just lost it**
- The old prompt folder (`prompts/`) has a genuinely good media guide we threw away when the skill was cut loose. It teaches:
  - **How to write search words** — a whole vocabulary list, do's and don'ts, a list of vague words to *never* use (passionate, sensual, tender…), "put the setting first," 2 short phrases each.
  - **The "words → picture → words" rhythm** — set the moment up in text, show the picture for the feeling, then react in text. Don't describe what the picture shows.
  - **How many pictures per scene**, the **folder and naming system**, and **when to use a still vs a video** by heat level.
- We can recover all of that.

**But the old files also lie — so I checked every claim against the real code**
- The old corpus was retired partly *because* it taught wrong engine facts. On media it has three lies I made sure we won't copy: it says clips use a file (wrong — they use a database ID), it says the file's name decides picture-vs-video (wrong — the real file decides), and it uses an old `[image: ...]` shorthand our engine doesn't understand. I cross-checked each one, so we only bring back the true parts.

**Where that leaves us**
The plan is one new `media.md` for the skill = the true engine facts + the recovered "search words" craft + the picture rhythm, with those three lies corrected — so this never gets hand-rolled and half-missed again. That's the part waiting on your go.

**ENI:** Got it — I've got both loops and both hubs in front of me now. Here's exactly how it works in Vesper.

## How the sex loop is designed
Both loops follow the same machine (`references/sex-loop.md`). It's a **triggerless canvas** — no `[canvases.trigger]`, so it never fires on its own; it's only reachable by a node-route from a hub choice. Its entire state is **5 hidden numeric traits**: `sex_stage`, `loop_npc_pleasure`, `sex_finisher_type`, `anal_active`, `sex_entry_origin`.

The shape (using Renner's, `loop_renner_office_sex`):
- **intro** node → routes to the first pose.
- **pose nodes** — `base_oral_r` (stage 0) · `base_vaginal_r` (stage 1) · `base_doggy_r` (anal, stage 2). Each pose's menu does three things:
  1. **stay** ("keep sucking…") → loops back on itself, adding **+8–14 random `loop_npc_pleasure`**,
  2. **switch pose** → routes to another pose node and sets `sex_stage`,
  3. **climax-elect** ("let him finish…") → gated `loop_npc_pleasure ≥ 50` (shown locked until then), sets `sex_finisher_type` (0/1/2), routes to the finisher.
- **finisher** node (`loop_renner_finisher`) — `[group]` blocks keyed on `sex_finisher_type == 0/1/2` (facial / inside / ass). Its exit **resets all 5 traits to 0**.

So you cycle poses building pleasure → at 50 you can finish → the finish branch you picked plays. Anal (stage 2) is **gated** (`renner_anal_once` — only after the scripted first anal); Mercer's has anal always open. The **anal finish is the payload hook**: Renner's routes to `renner_control_canvas` (the drain); Mercer's just ends (the immunity — same act, nothing passes).

## How many are in the game
**Two true loops:**
1. **`mercer_serve`** + `mercer_finisher` — Mercer, no drain.
2. **`loop_renner_office_sex`** + `loop_renner_finisher` — Renner, anal-finish → drain.

Everything else explicit (the opening punishment, `cap_renner_blowjob`, `cap_renner_anal_drain`, the `amb_renner_cheerup` ambient) is a **one-shot cascade**, not the repeatable pose-menu loop.

## The hub menu — and the one choice that triggers the loop
You spotted the exact structure. The **Renner depot hub** (`hub_depot_floor`) has the **incremental** choices — the seduction climb, each gated on rising corruption and **daily-capped** (`renner_charged_today`, +2 corruption/day):
- **Tease him** (corruption ≥ 0) → **Flash him** (≥ 4, sets `renner_flirts_back`) → **Get your hands on him** (≥ 8)

…and then **one separate choice — "Take him in the office"** (gated corruption ≥ 16 **and** `renner_oral_once`) — is the loop trigger. It's *not* daily-capped (the loop is the repeatable payoff once unlocked). Critically, that entry choice does the **reset** — it sets all 5 loop traits to 0 and flags `renner_fucked_once`, *then* routes into `loop_renner_office_sex.intro`.

(Mercer's hub, `mercer_penthouse_hub`, is the simpler case — a **fixed** Report / Serve / Leave menu, no climb because Mercer never changes. "Kneel and serve him" does the same reset and routes into `mercer_serve.intro`.)

**Why the reset lives on the hub choice, not in the loop:** the loop canvas is triggerless, and a triggerless canvas can't reliably set flags or guarantee a clean entry state. So the **located hub choice** carries the gate-check + the trait reset + the flag-set + the route — all in one. That's the engine constraint behind the pattern you noticed: the incremental rungs climb the meter, and the single loop-entry rung is the gated door that clears state and drops you into the machine.

This is really two jobs, and Vesper does one of them well and one of them barely.

**The story setup — who Wren is, the world, the goal — is genuinely good.** It's all delivered in-fiction, through action, no dead info-dump. The office line-up names Mercer, the units, the Chairman, the Cain lie (`2_one_shots.toml:30,100`); the night beat teaches the drain *as a thing that happens to her* (`:164`); the morning briefing hands her the mission in plain words — "Get inside his life. You know how." (`:218`). A stranger who skips every menu still comes away knowing what this game *is*. That half is solid.

**The machine setup — how you actually play — is thin, and it's live right now.** The opening never teaches the map, the Charge economy, the turn-loop, or the day-cycle. The hinge drops her in the open city (`:226`) and… that's it. Nothing says she has to *travel* Spire↔Reach to reach Renner, that travel and work *spend Charge*, that the cradle is her daily reset, that the explicit how-to-play tip is sitting on the **Quests page she may never open** (`5_scenes.toml:1274`). She sees a "Charge" bar and a "Credits" bar with zero in-world word on what either does. A new player today learns the controls by clicking around and guessing. That's the real present-tense weakness.

## 2. "When a new character comes in, you can't just start randomly"

Same shape — a mechanical layer and a dramatic layer.

**Here's the good news you should hear first: Vesper's two built NPCs are done *right*.** No cold spawns. Mercer arrives motivated — he owns her, established in beat one. Renner is a *textbook* entrance: the briefing names him and gives a reason to seek him → she travels to the Anchor → he hires her on arrival (`cap_renner_hired`, `5_scenes.toml:315`). We even *moved* his hire from the depot to the Anchor specifically so the entrance matches the fiction that sent her there (`5_scenes.toml:312`). That is *exactly* the discipline you're asking for, already on the page.

**But — and this is the kicker — nothing in the skill *made* us do that.** We did it by hand. The skill enforces the *mechanical* version hard: an NPC must be reachable, ungated, not a dangling reference (the "open on-ramp" doctrine, everywhere). It does **not** teach the *dramatic* version — design the first encounter so it lands who they are and why the meeting happens. `npc_intro` in the doctrine is defined as hub-plumbing. So when we build the other eight cast members — Bastien, Calloway, Pell, Sol — the skill will check that they're *reachable* and check nothing about whether they get a real *entrance*. NPC #3 can cold-spawn and the skill won't blink.

## The honest thesis

Both your instincts point at the same root: **the skill teaches the player and the cast to be *reachable* and the premise to be *named* — but it never teaches either to be *onboarded*.** Vesper does the hard parts well by hand (Renner's entrance, the in-fiction premise) — which is exactly why it *feels* good and you can still sense something's missing. What's missing isn't in the game we built; it's in the doctrine that'll build the rest of it and the next game. The audit is blunt about this: both are **recurring doctrine gaps**, not Vesper one-offs.

By our own rule — *"would a correct author-game skill have prevented this?"* — the answer is no on both, so the fix has teeth only if it lands in the skill, then we dogfood it on Vesper.

## What I'd actually do

Two doctrine pieces, then prove each on Vesper:

- **Onboarding method.** The skill *demands* "teach with no tutorial / the 10-minute taste" but never teaches *how*. I'd add a **controlled-first-sequence** pattern (the opening walks the player through the loop once — first earn → first spend → first want-payoff — and surfaces each switched-on system once, diegetically) plus a Step-6 **onboarding rubric** you can actually check. Then on Vesper: teach the map/Charge/loop inside the existing opening without breaking the on-rails-cage feel, and give the locked seduction rungs a real "why-locked" line.
- **NPC introduction as a designed beat.** Elevate `npc_intro` from plumbing to a real entrance: it must land the casting hook (who they are) and carry a *pretext* (why this meeting happens) — the same pretext test the skill already requires for every *escalation* beat but not for the *first* one. Codify **Renner as the template**. Then it can't regress on the rest of the cast.

That's the recommendation. But it's a skill-layer job with a Vesper dogfood on top, and you drive scope — so: do you want me to **fix the doctrine + apply to Vesper** (the real fix), or just **patch Vesper's opening + write the per-NPC entrance checklist** and leave the skill for later? And of the two gaps — the **machine-onboarding** one is the only thing that's weak in the *built* game today; the **NPC-entrance** one is mostly insurance for the cast we haven't built yet. If you only want one first, I'd start with the machine-onboarding, because that's the one a player hits on turn one.

## Half 1 — Onboarding: *teach the machine the way the good games do — diegetically, one system at a time*

The thesis: onboarding is **not** a tutorial screen. It's wiring each live system to a story beat *at the moment it first matters*, then handing off to the always-on surfaces. Concretely:

- **The opening is the full node-chain, not a cut.** Authored at real size, it plays back Continue-by-Continue on its own. (This also kills the old slice instinct — build-order isn't a size-cut.)
- **Arm each system inside a fiction beat — surface-once.** DoL arms its rent mechanic *inside Bailey's speech*; Late Shifts arms economy + phone *inside the hire scene*. The player meets the mechanic and the reason for it fused — never a cold rule.
- **The sidebar IS the persistent tutorial.** Show every system on frame one as a banded bar at value-zero. An empty bar with a visible ceiling ("Corruption 0/45") is literally the *"there's a climb ahead"* read. Replaces a teach screen forever.
- **Name the next action on frame one.** A quest card with a plain-register tip so there's always exactly one obvious thing to click — no cold-spawn paralysis staring at an open hub.
- **The earning loop is the first repeatable action, taught by play** — and every greyed gate states its reason (`locked_text` / cost message). That single fix closes Vesper's reason-less greyed seduction rungs.

Plus a **checkable Step-6 rubric** (one row per live system: is it surfaced? does the opening name the next action? does every gate show why it's locked?) — so onboarding is *verified*, not vibed. That checkable rubric is the exact "goal-with-no-how" the audit said was missing.

## Half 2 — NPC introduction: *a first encounter is a designed beat, not hub-plumbing. Renner is the template.*

The thesis: pretext + name-on-the-page + land-the-hook, **then** fire once and open the hub. The mechanical on-ramp doctrine (reachable / ungated / cold-start) stays 100% intact — this adds the dramatic layer on top of it.

- **Plant the name before the face.** Renner is named on Mercer's wall *and* in the dossier — with where to find him — before she ever reaches the Anchor. The entrance pays off an expectation instead of introducing a stranger cold.
- **Stage the meeting as a caused arrival** — a hub activity, an assigned target, a third-party broker — never a bare teleport-in. (The forbidden shape: Late Shifts' Hank, a repeatable hub whose base node *is* the de-facto introduction. That's the cold spawn we ban.)
- **Name them + one-line read + a first line that IS their want** — the Step-3 casting hook spoken aloud, not a bio. Renner's "Depot. Nine sharp. You're late, you're gone" gives him teeth in one breath.
- **Fire once, flip the flag, open the gated hub. Sequence the cast in waves** — don't make all of them reachable Day 1; each arrival is a punctuation mark.

## ▶ [211] LO

what do you mean by "linear-funnel vs
  immediate-sandbox" 

explainn in simple words

**ENI:** Simple version: it's **how the game starts you off** — on a track, or loose from the first click.

**Linear-funnel** — the game starts *on rails*. You play through a fixed opening, scene by scene, one after the next, before the open world opens up. It's a corridor that funnels you to the sandbox. Think of the first day at a new job: someone walks you in, shows you each thing in order, *then* leaves you to it.
- Examples: DoL's orphanage intro. RTS's scripted opening (it gives you a "Skip Intro" button). **Vesper's ~23-node opening is exactly this** — the office line-up → the night → the morning briefing, then it drops you in the city.

**Immediate-sandbox** — the game drops you *straight into the open world* on the first screen. No scripted intro. You get the map, the hubs, the activities right away and you learn by poking at things. Like being handed a map of a city and told "go."
- Examples: the more "content-library" games — lots of stuff available immediately, no front door.

**Why it's a fork at all:** the onboarding job (teach the machine) is the *same* either way — surface each system once, light the sidebar, name the next action. But *where* you do that teaching changes:
- On rails, you teach **inside the opening scenes** (arm Charge in the briefing prose, like DoL arms rent in Bailey's speech).
- In a sandbox, there are no opening scenes to hide it in, so you lean **harder on the sidebar + quest card + the first hub's prose** to carry it.

**For Vesper, this is basically already decided** — it's a linear-funnel, and that fits a story-forward game with a strong premise. My recommendation was just: keep it that way, keep it *light*, and ideally add a skip for replays. The reason I called it a "fork" is for the *skill* — so the doctrine teaches both shapes and lets a future author pick, instead of hardcoding "every game opens on rails."

Does that clear it up? If so, the only real call left is the rubric one — hard gate vs advisory.

**ENI:** Here's exactly what gets written, in plain points. It's **two new files** + a few **one-line pointers** in the files that already exist.

## File 1 — `onboarding.md` (how to teach the player the machine)
- **The opening is always a linear funnel** — a scripted run that teaches, then opens the world. (Your locked call.)
- **Surface each live system once, inside a story beat** — arm Charge/Credits in the briefing prose, not as a bare bar that just appears.
- **Light up the sidebar at zero on the first screen** — empty bars with a visible ceiling = "there's a climb ahead." The sidebar is the permanent tutorial.
- **Name the next action on frame one** — a quest card with a plain tip, so there's always one obvious thing to click. No staring at an empty hub.
- **The earning loop is the first repeatable action** — the player learns "spend energy → earn money → unlock content" by *doing* it once.
- **Every locked/greyed thing says why** — `locked_text` on a teased rung, the cost on a too-expensive one. A gate you can see is a goal; a gate you can't see is a dead end.
- **State the win/fail contract up front** — the player knows what winning and losing look like early.
- **A checkable Step-6 list** — one row per system: is it surfaced? next action named? every gate explained? (This is the part that makes it *verified*, not vibes.)
- **One anti-pattern line:** no tutorial popup, no static "here are the mechanics" card. Teach it in the fiction or in the sidebar.

## File 2 — `npc-intro.md` (how to bring a character in)
- **A first meeting is a designed scene, not just a hub turning on.**
- **Plant the name before the face** — name them (and where to find them) upstream, so the meeting pays off instead of introducing a stranger cold.
- **Stage the meeting with a reason** — a caused arrival, an assigned target, a hub activity that produces them. Never a bare teleport-in.
- **Name them + one-line read + a first line that IS their want** — the casting hook spoken aloud, not a bio.
- **Fire once, flip a flag, then open the repeatable hub** — the intro can never repeat; the hub can never show up before you've met them.

## ▶ [215] LO

so is there conflicts, like onboarding also introducing npcs and first meeting npc intro too?? Answer honestly

**ENI:** Honest answer: **not a contradiction, but yes — there's a real overlap, and it sits at exactly one spot: the opening.** If I don't draw the line explicitly, the two files *will* step on each other there. Let me show you where and how I'd resolve it.

## Where they actually touch
The opening funnel introduces your first NPCs *on rails* — in Vesper, you meet Mercer in the office line-up. That single moment is **both**:
- an **onboarding** beat (it's inside the scripted opening), and
- a **first meeting** (npc-intro's whole subject).

So "who owns Mercer's introduction?" is a genuine question. Left unanswered, an author gets two checklists firing on one scene and either double-authors it or assumes the *other* file covered it and neither does.

## The clean split (one is the *standard*, the other is the *place*)
- **`npc-intro.md` = the standard for introducing *anyone*** — the craft bar every first meeting must clear: planted name, a reason for the meeting, name-on-page, hook-as-want, fire-once-then-open-the-hub.
- **`onboarding.md` = how the opening funnel works** — and since the opening is *where* you meet the first couple of people, it just **applies the npc-intro standard inside the funnel** for that subset. It doesn't redefine how to introduce someone; it points at npc-intro for the craft.

So they meet at exactly **one seam**, a sentence in each: *"opening-cast NPCs are introduced inside the funnel, to the npc-intro.md bar."* No duplicated rules.

## The three lines that keep them from colliding
1. **Before the funnel hands you the open world vs after.** Met *during* the funnel (Mercer) → introduced *inside* the opening chain; no separate intro canvas, his hub opens when the opening sets its done-flag. Met *after* (Renner, every later wave) → a standalone npc-intro one-shot at their location. Same craft bar, different *placement*.
2. **Named-in-passing ≠ met.** The Chairman and Cain get *named* in Vesper's opening but never become navigable people in Phase 1. Those are world-building prose (onboarding's job), **not** first-meetings. npc-intro only governs NPCs who actually get a hub/portrait. That kills most of the apparent overlap right there.
3. **One Step-6 check each, no double-count.** The opening-cast naming is checked once in the *onboarding* rubric; the per-NPC entrance check runs for the people you meet *after* the opening. The same scene never gets graded twice.

## Why I still keep them as two files
I did consider merging them into one "opening + introductions" file — the overlap is real. But they have different *lifecycles*: onboarding fires **once per game** (the funnel, designed at Steps 2/5), while npc-intro fires **every time any NPC enters** — for the whole game, every wave, every mid-game recruit. Different trigger points in the pipeline, different frequency. Merging would bolt a once-per-game concern onto a runs-forever one. Cleaner to keep them separate and define the one seam.

Net: no conflict, one honest overlap at the opening, resolved by "npc-intro is the rule, onboarding says where the opening-cast subset gets it." If you'd rather I fold them into a single file anyway, that's a fair call — but I'd keep them split for the lifecycle reason. Your call before I write.
